riskReasons: RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden and a documented living collection consistently support the accepted name and Acer palmatum placement.
The compact red dissectum habit and scarlet-to-burgundy seasonal sequence are compatible across the reviewed sources.
Several red laceleaf cultivars are visually similar, but the comparison risk is bounded and does not create a duplicate or synonym dispute.

duplicateCheck.notes: Compared with RC-001–RC-010 and all other owner-approved Catalogue assignments. ‘Red Dragon’ is distinct from RC-004 ‘Crimson Queen’ and from CUL-000013 ‘Inaba-shidare’, CUL-000021 ‘Tamukeyama’ and CUL-000022 ‘Orangeola’. The reviewed sources support a compact upright-pendulous to cascading red dissectum with a scarlet spring flush, burgundy summer foliage and scarlet autumn colour. C0 resolves as unique.

identityNotes: The Atlas uses Acer palmatum ‘Red Dragon’. Var. dissectum and Dissectum Group formulations are horticultural placement and search variants, not separate cultivar identities. The common English words “red dragon” occur outside maples, so taxon-qualified context is required in search and media review.

content.summary: A compact red laceleaf Japanese maple forming an upright-pendulous to cascading mound, with deeply cut foliage that opens scarlet or cherry red, matures to burgundy and returns to brilliant scarlet or crimson in autumn.
content.habit: Compact, well-branched deciduous shrub or small tree with an upright-pendulous to cascading mound. Institutional profiles generally place it around 1.5–2.5 m high and wide over time.
content.leafForm: Fine dissectum foliage with seven sharply pointed lobes cut deeply to the leaf base; Missouri Botanical Garden also notes deeply toothed sub-lobes and purple leaf stalks.

seasonal.spring: Leaves emerge bright scarlet to cherry red; inconspicuous reddish-purple flowers may be followed by purple winged fruits.
seasonal.summer: Foliage darkens to deep burgundy and is reported to retain red colour comparatively well, though heat, exposure and moisture influence intensity.
seasonal.autumn: Leaves change to flaming scarlet or crimson red.

size.qualifier: RHS gives 1.5–2.5 m high and wide at 10–20 years; Missouri Botanical Garden gives 6–8 ft high and wide. Use as an approximate garden range, not a fixed maximum.

content.cultivation: Grow in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with shelter from strong winds. In hotter regions, provide afternoon shade and reliable moisture to reduce scorch. Missouri Botanical Garden reports better sun performance than many dissectum types, but this remains climate- and moisture-dependent rather than a guarantee.
content.diagnostic: Compare with RC-004 ‘Crimson Queen’ and the red dissectum Catalogue profiles ‘Inaba-shidare’, ‘Tamukeyama’ and ‘Orangeola’. ‘Red Dragon’ is commonly presented as compact, with a scarlet spring flush and burgundy summer foliage, but colour and cascading form alone cannot authenticate a clone.
content.confidence: High confidence in accepted name, taxon, dissected leaf form and broad scarlet–burgundy–scarlet sequence; moderate confidence in comparative sun tolerance and visual separation from other red dissectums because these traits vary with site and are not clonal proof.
content.unresolvedIssue: No single visual trait reliably authenticates ‘Red Dragon’ against all other red dissectum cultivars, and the reported comparative sun tolerance has not been evaluated here across climates.
